scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Siva Tau was composed in the 1980s as a new war chant for Samoan national sports teams, replacing the traditional Maulu'ulu Moa dance.
It was first performed in 1991 by the Manu Samoa rugby union team at the Rugby World Cup.
The change aimed to provide a more aggressive and effective pre-match ritual to psych up players and assert Samoan identity on the international stage.
on_screen: Map: Samoa · Oceania

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Siva Tau is performed before international rugby union and rugby league matches, as well as Australian rules football matches involving Samoan national teams.
It functions as a war challenge to opponents, projecting aggression, strength, and Samoan cultural pride.
Leading the dance is considered an honor and a symbol of identity for the players.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The Siva Tau is primarily a vocal chant performed a cappella by the team members.
It features rhythmic chanting with a strong, commanding tone.

The Siva Tau features a powerful, rhythmic vocal chant performed by multiple voices in unison, punctuated by sharp knee strikes and vigorous arm gestures that mimic spear handling, creating an atmosphere of martial intensity.

scenes.title: The people
narration: No specific individuals are named as creators or prominent performers of the Siva Tau in the sources.
A more aggressive version of the Siva Tau was used by the Manu Samoa team during the 2007 Rugby World Cup but was later dropped in favor of the original.
The Siva Tau is part of the Polynesian war dance tradition, related to other Pacific dances such as the New Zealand haka, the Fijian cibi, and the Tongan kailao.
